title: Prayer for Christian unity (18–25 January)
hookLine: a week when churches pray for each other

lines: A PRAYER WITH ANOTHER CHURCH'S NAME IN IT.
cards: On a weeknight in January, a Lutheran pastor reads a prayer out loud, and the name in it belongs to the Catholic parish two streets over.
Across town, an Orthodox priest asks God's blessing on a Pentecostal church that meets in a former shop. A Methodist choir sings in a Baptist chapel, and nobody tries to sign anybody up.
For one week, churches that disagree about baptism, bishops and bread pray for each other by name. Not to settle the arguments. Just to pray.
Behind that week sits a single night, a table, and a prayer Jesus prays for people who will come after his friends.

teach.h: THE NIGHT BEFORE, A LONG PRAYER.
teach.b: John's Gospel slows right down on the night before Jesus dies. After the supper and the long talk, he looks up and prays, and all of chapter seventeen is that prayer.
Partway through, he turns from the friends in the room to everyone who will come after them.

teach.h: THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me."
It isn't a rule; nobody is ordered to be one. It's a request, made to God. And notice the pattern: one the way the Father and the Son are one.
Not identical, not merged into a single shape. Close, and turned toward each other. Churches don't use it to pretend their differences are gone.

Catholics, Orthodox Christians and Protestants still hold different views about how the church is ordered, who presides at communion, and what unity would finally look like. Some hope for one visible church.

Some think unity already exists underneath the different names. The week doesn't decide between them. It asks each church to pray the prayer Jesus prayed, and to say the other church's name while doing it.
And the last clause: that the world may believe. How Christians treat each other is part of how anyone hears the message. A family that only argues is hard to listen to.

how: During the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, churches of different traditions hold shared services, swap pulpits or choirs, and include one another by name in their prayers.

practice: Bring to mind a church you've never set foot in: the unfamiliar name on the corner, a chapel you pass on the bus, a congregation that worships in a language you don't speak.

Picture the door, the people going in, someone setting out chairs. If you pray, hold that church before God by name and ask good things for it; if you don't, simply wish it well, the people inside and the work they do.
